title: Composite-State Localization Beyond the External Landscape in Non-Hermitian Quasicrystals
authors: Tian Zhou, Xue-Bin Wang, Zhongmin Yang, Tao Liu
abstract: A composite excitation need not inherit the localization behavior of its constituents. We show that an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder realizes a controllable and reversible localization inversion between composite and unbound excitations, where internal configuration, rather than only the external potential, becomes a control parameter for localization. Opposite complex potentials on the two legs cancel at first order for a same-rung pair but act directly on separated particles, allowing extended composite states to persist while the unpaired sector becomes localized. A strong-coupling theory identifies the composite state as an emergent weakly modulated non-Hermitian quasicrystal generated by virtual unpaired configurations. Breaking the potential antisymmetry restores a direct modulation of the composite band and reverses the localization hierarchy. Engineering configuration-space pathways further stabilizes an extended composite band embedded within a localized continuum, the inverse of the conventional bound-state-in-the-continuum scenario. Our results establish internal configuration as a reversible control parameter for localization.
summary: This paper explores localization in interacting, non-Hermitian quasiperiodic systems, establishing that the binding configuration of particles dictates their transport properties. By analyzing effective Hamiltonians, the authors show a controllable 'localization inversion' where composite pairs remain extended even when individual unpaired particles become localized. This highlights internal interactions as a powerful control mechanism beyond external potentials.
main_problem: The study investigates whether composite excitations can exhibit localization behavior opposite to their constituent particles within a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic environment.
main_result: The paper demonstrates that internal particle configuration acts as a reversible control parameter, allowing for controllable localization inversion where the composite state remains extended while unpaired constituents localize.
method: The analysis uses effective Hamiltonian derivations via perturbation theory and diagnoses localization using the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) across varying system sizes.
model_or_system: The model is an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder hosting hard-core bosons, governed by a complex potential $V(\Delta\phi)$ and interaction terms $H_{	ext{int}}$.
key_observables: Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) for localization diagnosis; particle density profiles ($\langle n_{ eta,j} angle$); effective pair hopping ($J_{eff,j}$).
important_parameters: Non-Hermiticity strength ($h$); relative phase $\Delta\phi$; interaction strength $U_1$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the strongly interacting regime ($U_1 \gg |J|, |t|, |V|$) and assumes quasi-degeneracy for perturbation theory application.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate IPR evolution showing distinct localization paths for paired vs. unpaired states, confirming the persistence of an extended composite band embedded within a localized continuum across increasing system sizes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing the basic antisymmetric case ($\Delta\phi=0$) to deriving effective Hamiltonians for the pair sector using perturbation theory, culminating in demonstrating configuration-dependent localization inversion and stabilizing extended states via engineered interactions.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework showing how emergent collective behavior (the composite state) can decouple its transport properties from the single-particle physics dictated by external disorder or non-Hermiticity.

Particles occupying the same rung interact with strength U1. The upper and lower legs experience the complex quasiperiodic potentials Va,j = V cos(2παj + ih + ∆ϕ/2) and Vb,j = −V cos(2παj + ih −∆ϕ/2), respectively.

FIG. 2. (a) Evolution of the maximum (solid lines) and minimum (dashed lines) IPR of paired (light blue) and unpaired (vermilion) states as a function of the non-Hermitian strength h. Three characteristic localization transition points are identified: h1 ≃0.6, h2 ≃1.58, and h3 ≃2.37. The first two transitions correspond to the successive extended–mixed–localized evolution of the unpaired states, while the third transition marks the onset of localization of the paired states.
